summary: Can trend-following hedge fund returns be explained by option-like risk? Primitive trend-following strategy modelled as three-month lookback straddles on 26 futures markets, replicated by rolling standard straddles; compared with 407 CTA funds, 1985-1997 monthly data. Lookback straddle portfolios explain trend-follower returns (adjusted R2 47.9%) while standard asset benchmarks do not (about 1-8%); trend followers are long a convex, crisis-like payoff concentrated in currencies, bonds and commodities.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Hedge fund strategies typically generate option-like returns.
claims.claim: Hedge fund returns are typically option-like, so linear factor models on benchmark asset indices fit them poorly.
claims.testable: yes - nonlinearity of fund returns vs asset returns

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: We use lookback straddles to model trend-following strategies
claims.claim: Trend-following fund returns are modelled as returns on lookback straddles, which explain them better than standard asset indices.
claims.exact_rule: trend-following return = T-bill + long three-month lookback straddles on each market (details Section 2)

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Though standard straddles lead to similar empirical results, lookback straddles are theoretically closer to the concept of trend following.
claims.claim: Standard straddles give similar empirical results to lookback straddles; lookback straddles are chosen for theoretical closeness to trend following.
claims.reported_result: monthly lookback vs standard straddle correlation 0.86 for yen (Section 2); 0.834 for Swiss franc (Section 3.3)

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: This article received research support from the Foundation for Managed Derivatives Research and John W. Henry & Company.
claims.claim: Disclosure: research was supported by a managed-futures foundation and by John W. Henry & Company, a large trend-following CTA, a potential conflict to bear in mind.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Linear-factor models of investment styles using standard asset benchmarks, as in Sharpe (1992), are not designed to capture the nonlinear return features commonly found among hedge funds.
claims.claim: Sharpe-type linear style regressions on asset benchmarks cannot capture the nonlinear (option-like) return features of hedge funds.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: This may lead investors to conclude erroneously that there are no systematic risks.
claims.claim: Linear models can make hedge funds look as if they have no systematic risk, because the risk is nonlinear.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: A remedy is in Glosten and Jagannathan (1994), where they suggested using benchmark-style indices that have embedded option-like features.
claims.claim: Glosten and Jagannathan (1994): use benchmark indices with embedded option-like features to evaluate funds with nonlinear payoffs.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: By construction, these style factors captured much of the option-like features while preserving the general lack of correlation with standard asset benchmarks.
claims.claim: Fung and Hsieh (1997a) extracted hedge fund style factors that capture option-like features and are uncorrelated with standard benchmarks, but linking them to markets is hard because funds do not disclose positions.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: greatly limits the value of analyzing a general sample of many hedge funds
claims.claim: Hedge funds dynamically allocate across strategies with different nonlinear risks, so pooled samples blur risk; the authors instead study one identifiable strategy (trend following, CTA funds).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Trend following is a self-described strategy for the major- ity of commodity trading advisors (CTAs)
claims.claim: Trend following is the self-described strategy of most CTAs (Billingsley and Chance 1996), so CTA funds are used as the sample.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Grinblatt and Titman (1989) showed that a manager can generate positive Jensen’s alphas by selling call options
claims.claim: Footnote 3 evidence: linear alpha regressions mislead when payoffs are nonlinear (selling calls gives positive Jensen alpha; Merton 1981 market timing gives option-like returns; Treynor-Mazuy and Henriksson-Merton add nonlinear terms).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Fung and Hsieh (1997b) showed that the returns of CTA funds have one dominant style factor.
claims.claim: Principal component analysis of CTA funds shows one dominant style factor, interpreted as trend following; the model targets that factor and also helps explain other hedge funds that use trend following.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: State 1 consists of the worst months, and State 5 the best months.
claims.claim: Figure 1 (from Fung and Hsieh 1997b): sorting monthly MS World Equity returns into five states, six large trend-following funds earn positive returns in the worst and best states (about +4% in state 1 when world equities average about -9.5%; about +4.5% in state 5 when equities gain about +10%) and little in the middle.
claims.reported_result: Figure 1 read from chart: world equities by state about -9.5%, -2%, +1.3%, +4.4%, +10%; six trend followers about +4%, +2%, +1.3%, +2.8%, +4.5% monthly
claims.direction: trend followers behave like long straddle on world equities

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: the state-dependent beta estimates tend to be positive in up markets and nega- tive in down markets
claims.claim: Trend followers have low average beta to equities but beta is positive in up markets and negative in down markets, i.e. a convex, option-like payoff.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: must therefore have systematic risk, albeit in a nonlinear manner
claims.claim: Contingent-claim-like returns mean trend followers must bear systematic risk, which linear betas can understate or overstate (the LTCM case).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: We can therefore only theorize what trend followers do.
claims.claim: Caveat: trading rules are proprietary, so the model is a theoretical proxy, not a replication of any manager.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: While the S&P 500 lost 14.5% of its value, commodity funds generally had positive returns.
claims.claim: Out-of-sample support (footnote 6): in August 1998 the S&P 500 fell 14.5% while commodity funds generally gained; per Barron's, 82% of 17 CTAs reporting to MAR were positive and 46 posted more than 10%.
claims.reported_result: Aug 1998: S&P 500 -14.5%; 82% of CTAs positive

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Average monthly returns of six large trend-following funds in
claims.claim: Figure 1 caption: average monthly returns of six large trend-following funds in five MS world equity market states; source Fung and Hsieh (1997a).
claims.reported_result: see Figure 1 claim

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Trend followers can converge onto the same “trend” for different reasons and have very different “entry and exit” points.
claims.claim: Individual trend followers differ in entry and exit rules, so a stylised aggregate strategy is needed to capture the common payoff while avoiding idiosyncrasies.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: has the same payout as a structured option known as the “lookback straddle.”
claims.claim: Primitive trend-following strategy (PTFS) is posited to have the same payout as a lookback straddle: long lookback call (buy at lowest price over life) plus lookback put (sell at highest price), paying the ex post maximum price range of the underlying.
claims.exact_rule: PTFS payout = S_max - S_min over the option life; cost = lookback straddle premium

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: which delivers the ex post maximum payout of any trend-following strategy
claims.claim: The lookback straddle gives the ex post maximum payout of any trend-following strategy, i.e. the perfect-foresight upper bound.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: trend followers should deliver returns resembling those of a portfolio of bills and lookback straddles
claims.claim: Prediction: trend-follower returns resemble bills plus a portfolio of lookback straddles.
claims.testable: yes - tested via regressions in Section 3

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: trend followers often make multiple entry and exit decisions over a
claims.claim: Footnote 7: the model excludes multiple entries and exits within the horizon that real trend followers make when volatility around a trend is high.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Rather, it is designed to capture the general characteristics of the entire family of trend-following strategies.
claims.claim: The option strategy is not tuned to replicate a specific trading rule (unlike earlier technical-rule studies) but to capture the general features of all trend-following strategies.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: This provides the key link between the returns of trend-following funds and standard asset markets.
claims.claim: The key empirical link: lookback straddle returns resemble trend-following fund returns, connecting funds to standard asset markets.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Given any asset, we show that the lookback straddle is better suited to capture the essence of trend-following strategies than a simple straddle.
claims.claim: Theory (Section 1, Appendix A): a lookback straddle captures trend following better than a standard straddle, which captures market timing.
claims.testable: partly - empirical difference small at monthly horizon

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: which is the return of a portfolio of bills and a call option on stocks
claims.claim: Merton (1981): with short-sale constraints a perfect market timer earns R + max{0, Z-R}, i.e. bills plus a call on stocks.
claims.exact_rule: R(t)+Max{0,Z(t)-R(t)}

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: which is the return of a portfolio of bills and a straddle on stocks.
claims.claim: Without short-sale constraints a perfect market timer earns R + max{0,Z-R} + max{0,R-Z}, bills plus a straddle on stocks (Merton 1981).
claims.exact_rule: R(t)+Max{0,Z(t)-R(t)}+Max{0,R(t)-Z(t)}

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Here we note the opportunistic nature of trend followers.
claims.claim: Trend followers allocate capital dynamically across markets in ways peculiar to their skill and technology, which complicates benchmarking.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: A trend is a series of asset prices that move persistently in one direction over a given time interval, where price changes exhibit posi- tive serial correlation.
claims.claim: Trend defined as persistent one-directional price movement with positive serial correlation of price changes; a trend follower trades in the direction of a developing pattern.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: The PTFS, on the other hand, attempts to capture the largest price movement during the time interval.
claims.claim: PMTS (market timer) payout is |S'-S| (initial vs end price); PTFS payout is S_max - S_min (largest movement inside the interval), so PTFS adds trades at the max and min.
claims.exact_rule: PMTS payout = |S_end - S_start|; PTFS payout = S_max - S_min; one trade per interval

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Consistent with the Merton (1981) framework, we restrict our strategies to complete a single trade over the given time interval.
claims.claim: Both primitive strategies complete a single trade per interval, following Merton (1981).
claims.exact_rule: one trade per interval

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Note that we are not advocating that markets trend. That is an empirical issue best deferred to another occasion.
claims.claim: Key caveat (footnote 9): the paper does not claim markets trend; it only models and risk-characterises trend-following funds, leaving the profitability or serial correlation of trends untested.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Capital allocation to the PMTS or PTFS is determined by comparing the payout of the respective strategy to the return of the risk-free asset.
claims.claim: Capital is split between the primitive strategy and the risk-free asset by comparing payout to the risk-free return (option premium vs bills); footnote 11 says the split also depends on risk preference.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Generally, market timers enter into a trade in anticipa- tion of a price move over a given time period, whereas trend followers trade
claims.claim: Market timers trade in anticipation of a move; trend followers trade only after observing certain price movements within the period (buying breakouts, selling breakdowns).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: if Merton’s (1981) assumptions were strictly imposed, the payout of the PTFS must equal that of the PMTS.
claims.claim: Footnote 10: under strict Merton assumptions PTFS and PMTS payouts coincide; the difference arises from path dependence.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: The terms buying breakouts and selling breakdowns are often used to describe trend followers.
claims.claim: Trend followers buy breakouts (price above recent high) and sell breakdowns (price below recent low).
claims.exact_rule: long when price breaks above recent high; short when below recent low (footnote 12)

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: we assume that the ex ante cost of the PMTS is the value of an at-the-money standard straddle
claims.claim: Costs of capturing the optimal payout cannot be estimated without the strategies, so the PMTS cost is assumed to be an at-the-money standard straddle and the PTFS cost a lookback straddle.
claims.exact_rule: PMTS = long ATM straddle; PTFS = long lookback straddle

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: In the next section, we will empirically create returns of the PTFS using lookback straddles on 26 different markets.
claims.claim: PTFS returns are built from lookback straddles on 26 markets.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: In comparison, the delta of the lookback straddle is given by
claims.claim: Black-Scholes deltas: standard straddle delta = 2N(a1)-1; lookback straddle delta is path dependent through the running minimum Q and maximum M (Equations 1-12); a derivation is available on request.
claims.exact_rule: delta_std = 2N(a1)-1, a1=[ln(S/X)+(r+0.5 sigma^2)T]/(sigma sqrt T); delta_LB per Eq. 3 with Q=min, M=max since inception

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Breakout means that the price of an asset moves above a recent high, and buying breakouts refers to the strategy of going long when a breakout happens.
claims.claim: Footnote 12: definitions of breakout and breakdown.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Here Q and M denote the minimum and maximum prices, respectively, of the asset since the inception of the lookback straddle.
claims.claim: Lookback delta uses Q = minimum and M = maximum price since inception; the key difference from a standard straddle is path dependency.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Consequently, as the investment horizon shrinks, the payouts of the two strategies converge.
claims.claim: PMTS and PTFS payouts are equal only if S_max and S_min occur at the start and end; they converge as the horizon shrinks and diverge as it lengthens.
claims.conditions: horizon: short -> same payout; long -> differ

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: For stock indices, we used the futures contracts on the S&P 500 (CME), Nikkei 225 (Osaka), FTSE 100 (LIFFE), DAX 30 (DTB),
claims.claim: Universe, financial markets: 5 stock index futures (S&P 500, Nikkei 225, FTSE 100, DAX 30, Australian All Ordinary), 5 bond futures (US 30y, UK Gilt, Bund, French 10y, Australian 10y), 4 currency futures (GBP, DEM, JPY, CHF), 6 three-month rate futures.
claims.exact_rule: stocks 5, bonds 5, currencies 4, 3-month rates 6 (26 markets total incl. commodities)
claims.data_needed: futures and options on CME, Osaka, LIFFE, DTB, SFE, MATIF, TIFFE, CBOT

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: For commodities, we used the futures contracts on soybean, wheat, and corn futures traded on the CBOT and gold, silver, and crude oil
claims.claim: Universe, commodities: soybean, wheat, corn (CBOT), gold, silver, crude oil (NYMEX).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Futures and option data on the DTB, MATIF, and Osaka were purchased from the Futures Industry Institute (FII).
claims.claim: Data: exchange-supplied or purchased futures and options settlement data plus Datastream futures (Appendix B).
claims.data_needed: exchange futures and option settlement prices

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: First, lookback options are not exchange-traded contracts, so we can- not directly observe their prices.
claims.claim: Lookback options are not traded, so their payout is replicated by rolling a pair of standard straddles (Goldman, Sosin, Gatto 1979).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: We use one strad- dle to lock in the high price of the underlying asset by rolling this straddle to a higher strike whenever the price of the underlying asset moves above the current strike.
claims.claim: Replication rule, high straddle: roll to a higher strike whenever the underlying exceeds the current strike so the final strike equals the running maximum.
claims.exact_rule: buy 2 ATM straddles at inception; straddle 1 rolled up whenever price > current strike

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: We use the other straddle to lock in the lowest price of the underlying asset by rolling the straddle to a lower strike whenever
claims.claim: Replication rule, low straddle: roll to a lower strike whenever the underlying falls below the current strike so the final strike equals the running minimum; the pair pays max minus min.
claims.exact_rule: straddle 2 rolled down whenever price < current strike; combined payout = S_max - S_min

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: An alternative replication strategy is a delta-hedging strategy using the underlying asset.
claims.claim: Footnote 14: delta hedging is an alternative but needs implied volatility of an untraded option.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Second, though the strategy of rolling standard straddles can replicate the payout of the lookback straddle, it may not perfectly replicate all the cash
claims.claim: Straddle rolls create extra cash flows that a true lookback straddle does not have; these are included in returns.
claims.conditions: cash flows from strike rolls included

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: This biases downward the returns of the PTFS.
claims.claim: Most US-exchange options are American style and cost more than European, biasing PTFS returns downward; LIFFE options are futures-style so unaffected.
claims.direction: PTFS returns understated for US options

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: we use the nearest-to-the- money options to approximate at-the-money options. The error is likely to be small.
claims.claim: Nearest-to-the-money options substitute for at-the-money (discrete strikes); authors judge the error small.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: we used lookback straddles with three months to expiration as close to the end of a quarter as possible to maintain consistency.
claims.claim: Horizon: three-month lookback straddles, set as close to quarter-end as possible, because financial options expire quarterly and commodity options mostly in Mar/Jun/Sep/Dec.
claims.exact_rule: three-month lookback straddle initiated near quarter-end; horizon dictated by option liquidity

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: In practice, we rolled the straddles only at the end of each trading day using the settlement prices of the options and the underlying assets.
claims.claim: Rolling is done daily at settlement prices, not continuously (tick data costly and asynchronous), then daily returns compound to monthly.
claims.exact_rule: roll straddles at daily settlement; aggregate daily returns to monthly

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: one each for stocks, bonds, three-month interest rates, currencies, and commodities.
claims.claim: Five PTFS portfolios (stocks, bonds, three-month rates, currencies, commodities) formed as equally weighted PTFSs.
claims.exact_rule: five equal-weighted portfolios of market PTFSs

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: a delta-hedging strategy can incur substantial transaction costs, as it requires dynamically changing the amount of the underlying asset every time its price changes.
claims.claim: Footnote 14: delta hedging would incur substantial transaction costs; straddle rolling needs far fewer transactions.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: Applying principal components analysis on all defunct and operating CTA funds, Fung and Hsieh (1997b) found a single dominant trading style.
claims.claim: PCA on defunct and operating CTA funds yields one dominant style (trend following); the study updates this with the Tass CTA database as of March 1998.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh

claims.claim: Of 1,304 funds, 407 are strongly correlated with the first principal component and form the representative trend-follower return series.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: This is likely to result in an upward bias, because the omitted defunct funds generally have poorer performance than surviving funds.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: mean, whereas the PTFS portfolios and most of the individual PTFSs do not.
claims.claim: Funds and PTFS share strong positive skewness, but funds have a significant positive mean (+1.37% monthly) while PTFS portfolios and most PTFSs do not; funds beat PTFS means except for the Swiss franc.

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
claims.quote: We defer further analysis of this implicit alpha in trend-following funds’ returns until Section 4.
claims.claim: The authors flag a positive implicit alpha in trend-following funds relative to PTFS, deferring analysis (Section 4 does not actually quantify it).

claims.speaker: William Fung; David A. Hsieh
